improve.title: St Mary's Old Church, Clophill – 1963 'Black Mass' desecration
improve.desc: The 14th-century church was abandoned in 1848 when a new St Mary's was built in the village, and fell into ruin. In March 1963 bones from a disturbed 18th-century grave were found laid out inside the ruin in what the press called Black Mass fashion, with cockerel feathers and red-painted crosses on the walls; further grave disturbances were reported in the following weeks. No one was charged. Students later admitted killing a cockerel there in 1961 as a prank, and the 'sacrifice' framing probably owed much to Dennis Wheatley's novels; the ruin is now a consolidated, Grade II-listed scheduled monument.

add_sources.name: Historic England – Church of St Mary the Virgin (list entry 1113735)
Bedfordshire Archives – Old St Mary's Church, Clophill

improve.title: Castle Rising Castle – effigies and sheep's heart
improve.desc: On 13 September 1963 a workman arriving for renovation work found two human effigies, one male and one female, nailed to the castle door, with a soot-blackened sheep's heart fixed between them by hawthorn twigs; two occult symbols had been drawn on the ground nearby, apparently in soot. It was the first of three linked finds around King's Lynn (Castle Rising, Bawsey, Babingley) over the winter of 1963–64. No one was ever identified.

improve.title: Bawsey ruined church – heart, black circle and candle
improve.desc: Roughly four months after the Castle Rising find (around January 1964), a soot-blackened sheep's heart was found nailed with hawthorn twigs to a wall of the ruined Norman church of St James on its hillock at Bawsey, about three miles away. Beside it was a black circle with a black wax candle at its centre; this time there were no effigies. Nobody was identified. The pin is now on the listed ruin itself.

add_sources.name: Historic England – Ruins of Church of St James, Bawsey (list entry 1077664)
Norfolk Heritage Explorer – NHER 3328, St James' Church, Bawsey

improve.title: Babingley ruined church – ritual objects gathered in tower
improve.desc: In February 1964 a local boy fishing in the nearby river explored the ruined church of St Felix at Babingley and found all three sets of ritual objects from Castle Rising and Bawsey (effigies, hearts and candle) collected together inside the tower. The find made national news, but the culprit was never identified. The pin is on the scheduled ruin, not the later thatched mission chapel by the A149.

add_sources.name: Historic England – St Felix's Church, Babingley (scheduled monument 1020767)
Norfolk Heritage Explorer – NHER 55921, St Felix' Church, Babingley

improve.title: St James's ruined church, Bix Bottom
improve.desc: The roofless Norman church of St James in a quiet Chiltern valley was abandoned in the 1870s. It is said to have drawn witchcraft and modern-pagan devotees from about 1925 and gained a sinister reputation after appearing in the occult films The Witches (1966) and The Blood on Satan's Claw (1971). No dated ritual incident is confirmed in the sources. The pin is now on the listed ruin.

add_sources.name: British Listed Buildings – Ruins of Church of St James, Bix and Assendon

improve.title: Highgate Cemetery – 'Highgate Vampire' and black-magic claims
improve.desc: Letters to the Hampstead and Highgate Express in February 1970 about a 'grey figure' grew into a media frenzy; after ITV broadcast interviews on 13 March 1970 a crowd of would-be vampire hunters climbed into the locked cemetery the same night. On 1 August 1970 the charred, headless remains of a woman were found near the catacombs and police reportedly suspected black magic. In 1974 one of the self-styled hunters was jailed for damaging memorials and interfering with remains, while insisting Satanists were to blame. Folklorists treat the 'vampire' as a press-fuelled legend driven by a rivalry between two occultists.

improve.title: Hellfire Caves, West Wycombe
improve.desc: Sir Francis Dashwood had the chalk caves dug in 1748–52, partly as poor relief, using the spoil to build the West Wycombe–High Wycombe road. His club (the 'Hellfire Club' name came later) met there in the 1750s and early 1760s after leaving Medmenham. Contemporary rumour spoke of devil-worship and black masses, but the most reliable account (Horace Walpole) describes 'rigorously pagan' revels to Bacchus and Venus. The Inner Temple lies beyond an underground 'River Styx', reputedly beneath St Lawrence's Church; the caves have been a tourist attraction since 1951.

improve.title: Medmenham Abbey – the 'Monks of Medmenham'
improve.desc: Dashwood leased the ruined Cistercian abbey from the Duffield family and remodelled it as the meeting place of his 'Monks of Medmenham', later called the Hellfire Club. The club was accused of obscene parodies of religious rites and was in disrepute by 1762, by which time meetings had moved to the West Wycombe caves. The house is now a private Grade II-listed residence and not open to the public.

improve.title: Montpelier Hill – Dublin Hellfire Club lodge
improve.desc: Speaker William Conolly built the hunting lodge on the summit around 1725, partly using stones from a prehistoric cairn; after the slate roof blew off he replaced it with the stone vault that survives. The Irish Hellfire Club, founded around 1737 by Richard Parsons, 1st Earl of Rosse, and the painter James Worsdale, is linked to the lodge by tradition only. Tales of a cloven-hoofed card player, a black-cat mascot and a chair kept for the Devil are unverifiable folklore. Excavation in October 2016 revealed a large passage tomb beneath the ruin.

add_sources.name: Abarta Heritage – Hellfire Club Archaeological Project
Kilkenny Castle – Drunkenness, debauchery and devil worship: Ireland's Hellfire Clubs

improve.title: Boleskine House – Crowley's Abramelin working
improve.desc: Crowley bought Boleskine from the Fraser family in 1899 to perform the Abramelin operation, a months-long ritual to contact one's Holy Guardian Angel that also involves binding demonic princes; legend says he abandoned it without banishing them. He left in 1913. Jimmy Page owned the house from 1970 to 1992. Fires in December 2015 and July 2019 (the latter suspected arson) gutted it; the Boleskine House Foundation bought the ruin in 2019 and the restored house re-opened to the public in April 2026.

add_sources.name: Wikipedia – Boleskine House

improve.title: Chanctonbury Ring – Devil-summoning hilltop
improve.desc: Legend says the Devil, who made the Ring, appears if you run seven times anticlockwise round the trees, offering a bowl of soup or porridge for your soul; the story's first known printing is 1909. Crowley and Victor Neuburg (who lived in Steyning) reportedly regarded it as a 'place of power'. Inside the Iron Age fort stood two Romano-British temples, one possibly linked to a boar cult. The Great Storm of 1987 felled most of the 1760s beeches.

improve.title: Rollright Stones – witches' coven lore and modern rites
improve.desc: Folklore says a witch turned a would-be king and his men into the King Stone and the King's Men circle, and the stones were long linked with witches' gatherings. In the 20th century the site became important to modern witchcraft and pagan groups, who still hold rites there; ribbons and clooties are tied to the nearby tree. The pin is now on the King's Men circle.

improve.title: Malkin Tower Farm, Blacko – Pendle witches' Good Friday meeting
improve.desc: On Good Friday, 10 April 1612, friends of the Demdike family allegedly met at Malkin Tower, the home of Elizabeth Southerns ('Old Demdike'), supposedly to plot freeing jailed relatives by blowing up Lancaster Castle. Magistrate Roger Nowell treated it as a witches' sabbat, and it triggered the Pendle trials. The tower's site is unknown: Malkin Tower Farm at Blacko rests on a hollow called Mawkin Hole and old masonry, but it lies several miles from places named at the trial; the 2011 Lower Black Moss cottage and land near Newchurch are rival candidates. Coordinates remain approximate.

add_sources.name: Forest of Bowland AONB – Malkin Tower report (PDF)

improve.title: Lancaster Castle – Pendle witch trials
improve.desc: The Pendle accused were held in Lancaster Castle's gaol and tried at the Lancaster Assizes on 18–19 August 1612 before Sir Edward Bromley; the clerk Thomas Potts published the proceedings in 1613. Ten of the Pendle accused were convicted and hanged. At the same assizes the three Samlesbury women were acquitted when their young accuser admitted she had been coached by a Catholic priest.

add_sources.name: Lancaster Castle – Lancashire witch trials
Wikipedia – Samlesbury witches

improve.title: Meon Hill – 1945 'witchcraft murder'
improve.desc: On 14 February 1945 an elderly farm labourer from Lower Quinton was found killed in a field called Hillground on the slopes of Meon Hill, pinned to the ground with a pitchfork and slashed with a hook. Chief Inspector Robert Fabian of Scotland Yard suspected the farmer he worked for, but there was not enough evidence; his 1945 reports make no mention of witchcraft, and the 'pagan rite' interpretation appeared in his writing only years later and was disputed by Gerald Gardner. It remains Warwickshire's oldest unsolved murder. The pin is now on the summit (approx).

add_sources.name: Wikipedia – Killing of Charles Walton

improve.title: Hagley Wood – 'Bella in the Wych Elm'
improve.desc: On 18 April 1943 four boys found a skull in a hollow wych elm in Hagley Wood; police recovered an almost complete female skeleton, with the hand bones found some distance away. The pathologist put her death in or before October 1941. In 1945 Margaret Murray suggested a 'Hand of Glory' ritual; spy theories followed, and graffiti asking 'Who put Bella/Luebella down the wych elm?' has appeared since 1944, later on the Hagley Obelisk. West Mercia Police closed a review in 2014; she has never been identified.

improve.title: St Peter's Church, Bramshaw – satanic graffiti amid livestock attacks
improve.desc: Between 16 and 20 November 2019 '666', inverted crosses and phallic symbols were spray-painted in gold on the door of St Peter's on Judds Hill, during a spate of New Forest livestock attacks (a sheep stabbed and daubed with pentagrams, a heifer and calves knifed). A 41-year-old Winchester man was arrested in January 2020 over sheep deaths at Cadnam and Bramshaw but was released. The church was targeted again in late 2022, when a dead fox was left on the doorstep and, on 12 December 2022, a dead cat was found tied to the flagpole. The pin is now on the church.

improve.title: Stagbury Hill trig point – five animal hearts and candles
improve.desc: In January 2023 five animal hearts were reported lying on top of a triangulation pillar near St Peter's Church, Bramshaw, with candles arranged in a circle around it, according to The Times as reported by the Christian Post (24 January 2023). Police said they were already patrolling the area because of earlier suspected satanist activity, including the dead cat on the church flagpole a month before. No arrests were reported. The press did not name the hill; the pin is now on the Stagbury Hill summit (OSM), about 2 km east of the church.

add_sources.name: Christian Post – Witchcraft suspected after 5 animal hearts found outside church

improve.title: Burley centenary stone – deer head and inverted cross
improve.desc: On 8 May 2024 a member of the public found a rotting deer's head with an upside-down cross on the centenary stone/milestone by Burley High Street; a local shopkeeper removed the head and kept the cross for police. The next day five sheep were reported stabbed at Cadnam, and Hampshire Police's Countryside Watch investigated both. Burley's witchcraft associations go back to Sybil Leek, who lived there in the 1950s. No arrests were reported.

add_sources.name: Bournemouth Buzz – Latest animal mutilation in string of disturbing incidents (Jan 2025)

improve.title: Vixen Tor – sheep arranged in a heptagram
improve.desc: In January 2005 seven sheep with broken necks were found about half a mile from a prehistoric stone site east of Vixen Tor, laid out in a seven-pointed star. In October 2005 six more were found at Moortown and near the tor with broken necks and eyes removed, four in a square and two beside a pattern of stones. Police linked the killings to the stone site, described as an old pagan meeting place, and investigated them as crimes; no one was identified.

add_sources.name: Stone Pages – news archive (Oct 2005, citing Western Daily Press)

improve.title: Moville church – '666' altar desecration
improve.desc: In late July / early August 2016 three Inishowen churches – at Moville, Malin and Culdaff (St Mary's, Bocan) – were entered, '666' was written on altar cloths and triangle-in-circle 'satanic' symbols were drawn inside. The incidents happened late in the evening or early morning; gardaí from Carndonagh investigated, and no arrests were reported. The priest at Moville declined to comment.

add_sources.name: TheJournal.ie – 'Satanic' attacks made on three churches in Donegal

improve.title: Malin church – '666' altar desecration
improve.desc: Malin was one of three Inishowen churches entered in late July / early August 2016: '666' was written on altar cloths and occult triangle-in-circle symbols drawn. The reports do not name the Malin church building, so the pin remains at village level (approx). Gardaí from Carndonagh investigated; no arrests were reported.

add_sources.name: TheJournal.ie – 'Satanic' attacks made on three churches in Donegal

improve.title: Culdaff church – '666' altar desecration
improve.desc: St Mary's Church at Bocan, near Culdaff, is believed to have been entered on Sunday 24 July 2016 between midday and 7pm, with the damage found the next day: symbols described as satanic were drawn on the altar cloths, as at Moville and Malin. The curate said nothing like it had happened in Culdaff before. Gardaí at Carndonagh investigated; no arrests were reported.

add_sources.name: TheJournal.ie – 'Satanic' attacks made on three churches in Donegal

improve.title: Kyteler's House, Kilkenny – Ireland's first witchcraft trial
improve.desc: In 1324 Bishop Richard de Ledrede of Ossory accused Dame Alice Kyteler and her associates of witchcraft and heresy, including denying Christ, sacrificing animals at crossroads to a demon lover called Robert (Robin Artisson) and bewitching her husbands. Her servant Petronilla de Meath was tortured, confessed, and was flogged and burned at the stake on 3 November 1324 – the first known execution for witchcraft in Ireland. Alice fled, possibly to England or Flanders, and vanishes from the record; her name lives on in Kyteler's Inn.

improve.title: St Andrew's Auld Kirk, North Berwick – 1590 witches' sabbat
improve.desc: Accused people in the North Berwick trials (1590–92) confessed under torture, often in Edinburgh's Old Tolbooth, to meeting the Devil in the Auld Kirk on Halloween night 1590 to raise storms against James VI and his Danish bride. More than 70 people were implicated; Agnes Sampson was strangled and burned, and Dr John Fian was burned on Edinburgh's Castlehill. The affair shaped James's Daemonologie (1597). The kirk ruins stand by the harbour.

improve.title: Witches' Mill, Castletown – Gardner's museum and coven
improve.desc: The 1828 windmill (rebuilt after a fire in 1848) was bought in the early 1950s by Cecil Williamson, who opened a museum of folklore and witchcraft there; he later sold it to Gerald Gardner, founder of Wicca, who ran it as the Museum of Magic and Witchcraft until his death in 1964. His successor Monique Wilson later sold the museum and its exhibits. The mill was listed in 1985 and converted into homes around 2000. It stands near the reputed home of the 17th-century 'Arbory witch'.

add_sources.name: IOM Today – Former witchcraft museum in windmill for sale
Wikipedia – Cecil Williamson

improve.title: St Beuno's Church, Pistyll – 1991 blood ritual
improve.desc: In September 1991 the churchwarden of this ancient pilgrim-route church on Llŷn found blood and cockerel feathers on the altar, blood sprinkled on the altar cloth and floor, and feathers stuck to the steps, though no bird was found. Visitors at the neighbouring caravan park had seen lights in the unlit church at about 2am and police at Nefyn were alerted. The Archdeacon of Meirionnydd (later Archbishop Barry Morgan) said it was too early to say what had happened; the church began locking its doors.

improve.title: St Mary's Church, Conwy – occult graffiti
improve.desc: In March 1987 occult symbols were scrawled on gravestones and church doors at St Mary and All Saints, Conwy, and at St Benedict's, Gyffin; a Conwy police sergeant blamed youngsters with a 'morbid interest in the occult'. It opened a run of late-1980s/early-1990s incidents around Conwy and Colwyn Bay that the press linked to a local coven. The pin is now on the listed church.

improve.title: St Benedict's Church, Gyffin – occult graffiti
improve.desc: In March 1987, the same month as the Conwy incident, occult symbols were scrawled on gravestones and church doors at St Benedict's, Gyffin, a medieval church known for its painted chancel ceiling. Police attributed both incidents to youngsters dabbling in the occult; no outcome was reported. The pin is now on the listed church.

improve.title: Holy Trinity Church, Llandudno – altar desecrated for 'occult rituals'
improve.desc: In June 1987 two 16-year-old boys urinated on the altar and were dealt with by Llandudno Juvenile Court; one told police he was a pagan and had stolen church ornaments for occult rituals. About two years later he appeared, aged 19 and living at Conwy Morfa, on ITV's Cook Report as a 'reformed Satanist', warning of black magic among local youngsters.

improve.title: Bryn-y-Maen parish church – inverted cross and occult slogans
improve.desc: In October 1991 a cross at the 'Cathedral of the Hills' (Christ Church, Bryn-y-Maen) was found turned upside down and occult slogans were daubed in the parish registers, two weeks after a break-in at St John's, Trofarth (which the vicar did not think was black-magic related). The church was closed to the public afterwards.

improve.title: Ffynnon Elian – the cursing well
improve.desc: Edward Lhuyd recorded healing offerings for sick children here around 1699, but by the later 18th century St Elian's well had become notorious as a cursing well: for a fee a keeper 'entered' a victim's name (on slate or paper, or with pins in a cork) into the water, and charged more to remove it. An 1818 account mentions a man indicted at the Flint Assizes for extorting money by pretending to free someone from the well. The well structure was destroyed around 1829 but the practice persisted for decades; the spring has since been restored by its owner. The pin is now from the Coflein record (NPRN 32271).

add_sources.name: Coflein – Ffynnon Elian (NPRN 32271)
RCAHMW – Welsh Witches
The Modern Antiquarian – the well at Llaneilion (1818 account)

improve.title: Denbigh town square – first Welsh witch execution
improve.desc: In 1594 Gwen ferch Ellis, a healer, was convicted of witchcraft after a charm written backwards was found at Gloddaeth, home of the justice Thomas Mostyn; gossip linked her to a woman who had quarrelled with him. She faced three indictments, including murder by witchcraft, and was hanged in Denbigh in October 1594 – the first person executed for witchcraft in Wales. One account places the gallows in the town square, another where Denbigh library now stands.

add_sources.name: Nation.Cymru – Curses, whispers and a demon fly

improve.title: Caernarfon Great Sessions – Llannor witch hangings
improve.desc: In 1622 the siblings Rhydderch ap Evan, Lowri ferch Evan and Agnes ferch Evan of Llannor on Llŷn were accused of causing the death of Marged Huws by witchcraft. They were tried at the Caernarfon Great Sessions, found guilty and hanged – one of only a handful of Welsh witchcraft cases to end in execution.

improve.title: Beaumaris – 1655 witch hanging
improve.desc: In 1655 Marged ferch Rhisiart (Margaret ferch Richard) was convicted at Beaumaris of cursing Gwen Meredith, who died, and was hanged. RCAHMW links the case to the Beaumaris Court House on Bulkeley Place, whose historic courtroom interior survives.

add_sources.name: RCAHMW – Welsh Witches

improve.title: Thor's Stone, Thurstaston Common – 'Viking altar' legend
improve.desc: Local legend says Norse settlers from nearby Thingwall used this large sandstone outcrop as an altar for sacrifices to Thor. The Thor association is generally regarded as a 19th-century antiquarian invention; the rock was shaped partly by quarrying. Morris dancers still mark May Day there. The pin is now on the stone (OS SJ 24474 84933).

new.title: St Bridget's Church, Dyserth – 1637 'sorcerer' accusations
new.desc: In 1638 witnesses in a Court of Arches pew dispute called a Dyserth parishioner a sorcerer, blaming him for bewitching two oxen at Easter 1637, a hog some twelve years earlier, and a neighbour's fatal illness. The claims were made to discredit him as a witness, and no witchcraft prosecution followed. Pin on the parish church.

Wikipedia – Witchcraft in early modern Wales

new.title: Llanasa – 1656 and 1690 witchcraft accusations
new.desc: In 1655–56 a Llanasa woman (from Picton) was jailed after a mariner claimed she had appeared to him surrounded by lanterns and led him to an alehouse where he fainted; she was bailed and more than thirty neighbours certified she had never been suspected of witchcraft, and no further action is recorded. In 1690 a local labourer was accused of maiming cattle after a fortune teller's hint, but sixteen gentry vouched for him and the case was dropped. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

new.title: Penley – 1657 witch trial (acquitted)
new.desc: Seven Penley residents accused a local woman of harming children, livestock and neighbours between 1649 and 1656. She was committed to gaol in 1657, escaped and was recaptured, and at the Flint Great Sessions on 28 September 1657 faced four indictments: the grand jury threw out two and a petty jury acquitted her on the others. She was discharged in April 1658. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

sources.name: National Library of Wales – Witchcraft in 17th-century Flintshire (part 2)
Wikipedia – Witchcraft in early modern Wales

new.title: St Michael's Church, Caerwys – inverted cross and pentacle
new.desc: The rector arrived for a Sunday service to find an inverted cross attached to the church door, a poster cut into a cross and pinned up, and noticeboard posters slashed with inverted crosses; a pentacle had been drawn on the wall a couple of weeks earlier. He called it 'a bit sinister' and worried young people were involved, but sought no punishment. The online report is undated.

sources.name: Daily Post – Concern at cultish acts

new.title: Caerwys 'witch stone' and Coed Trefraith witch legend
new.desc: Local informants told the antiquary Canon Ellis Davies that the largest of a group of limestone outcrops north of Caerwys, between Ty Coch and Coed y Ffrith, was a stake 'on which witches were burnt', with drilled holes for restraints; he judged them natural rocks. A separate oral tale tells of a herb-gathering woman in Coed Trefraith burned in her cottage by townsfolk after children's nightmares. Both are folklore; coordinates are approximate (Caerwys community).

sources.name: Myths, Legends & Oddities of North East Wales – Witchcraft in Caerwys

new.title: Wern Wen farm – hidden barn curse inscription
new.desc: During building recording by C.R. Archaeology, a carved inscription was found on a tie-beam of an early 19th-century barn at Wern Wen farm, deliberately hidden behind boards: 'MELLDIGEDIG + FYDDO + LLE + HWN + AMEN' – 'May this place be cursed. Amen'. It names no one; researchers suggest a departing tenant or disgruntled servant, and note the cursing well at Llanelian-yn-Rhos about five miles away. The 1845 tithe map lists the farm; coordinates are approximate (Llangystennin parish).

new.title: Gloddaeth Hall – the backwards charm of 1594
new.desc: A charm written backwards – taken as proof of harmful intent – was found at Gloddaeth, home of the justice Thomas Mostyn, and gossip tied it to the healer Gwen ferch Ellis, supposedly hired by a woman who had quarrelled with him. She was convicted and hanged at Denbigh in October 1594, the first person executed for witchcraft in Wales. The charm itself was never produced in evidence.

new.desc: The crematorium was vandalised on Halloween 1987; police had expected trouble after a 'macabre party' there the previous Halloween. The Daily Post placed it among the late-1980s run of Conwy-area incidents blamed on occult dabbling. No further details or outcome were reported.

new.desc: On New Year's Day 1990 a white wooden cross was taken from a young man's grave and its name plate removed; it turned up in a farmer's field nine days later. The theft fuelled village rumours of black magic, and the mayor spoke of 'countless fears and speculations'. No culprit was identified. Coordinates are town-level (approx).

new.desc: In May 1991 black fur and blood were found in Bodnant Road. The RSPCA blamed witchcraft as the summer solstice approached, saying cats are often skinned for ritual use. No investigation outcome was reported; the attribution was the RSPCA's speculation.

new.title: Swansea Devil – the 'cursed' statue facing St Mary's
new.desc: Local folklore says a rejected architect placed a three-foot devil ('Old Nick') on a building facing St Mary's Church when Blomfield's rebuilt church opened in 1896, prophesying it would burn – and the church was gutted in the 1941 Three Nights' Blitz. The fire was wartime bombing, and the revenge story is legend. The statue vanished in 1962, was found in a Gloucester garage in the 1980s and has been displayed at Swansea Museum since June 2019 (pin).

new.title: Allt-y-Rhiw – witch-bottle under a yew
new.desc: An 18th-century Buckley-ware jug, about a quarter filled with lead, was found buried at the foot of an old yew at Allt-y-Rhiw farmhouse near Llansilin. Amgueddfa Cymru interprets it as a witch-bottle used to seal or trap a troublesome spirit. Coordinates are for Llansilin (approx).

new.title: Foel Fawr Farm, Derwen – the bewitched churn
new.desc: In the 19th century the farmer's butter churn repeatedly failed and he suspected bewitchment. He called in a 'dyn hysbys'-style unbinder of spells from Gwyddelwern, who recited a counter-charm and bound rowan sprigs around the churn, after which butter came almost at once. Folk-witchcraft tradition; coordinates are for Derwen (approx).

new.desc: Two late Welsh witchcraft cases were heard at Haverfordwest Castle: in 1693 a Loveston woman accused of several harms, and in 1699 a Haverfordwest woman accused of making sailors sick. The outcomes are not recorded.

new.title: Montgomery – 1579 enchanted apple case

new.title: St Mark's Church, Newtown, Wigan – 'Azazel' graffiti
new.desc: On the morning of Thursday 27 June (year not stated in the online report; c. 2019) inverted crosses, a pentacle and the name 'Azazel' – a fallen angel – were found daubed in emulsion on the front doors of St Mark's Anglican church. Police appealed for information; no arrest was reported.

new.title: Samlesbury Hall – the 1612 Samlesbury witches
new.desc: Three Samlesbury women, one connected with the Southworths of Samlesbury Hall, were tried at Lancaster on 19 August 1612 after a 14-year-old relative accused them of witchcraft, including attending sabbats at Red Bank by the Ribble. All three were acquitted when she admitted she had been coached by a Jesuit priest; historians see the case as anti-Catholic propaganda. Pin on the hall.

new.title: Gallows Hill, Spital Boughton, Chester – 1656 witch hangings
new.desc: Chester's gallows stood on Gallows Hill (Barrel Well Hill) by the old leper hospital at Spital Boughton. Three Cheshire women were hanged at Boughton for witchcraft on 17 October 1654, and three more – Ellen Beach, Anne Osboston and Anne Thornton – on 15 October 1656, all maintaining their innocence. The site also has a memorial to the Catholic martyr John Plessington (1679). Coordinates approximate.

sources.name: Psychogeographic Review – Spital Boughton
National Library of Wales – Witchcraft in 17th-century Flintshire (part 1)

new.title: Wildboarclough – Mary Baguley, hanged 1675
new.desc: Mary Baguley of Wildboarclough was charged in April 1675 with bewitching to death a Wincle schoolmaster who fell ill, coughed blood and died. She was convicted and hanged that year, one of the last witchcraft trials in England to end in execution. Coordinates are hamlet-level (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Mary Baguley

new.title: Todmorden – Vodou veve with goat skull
new.desc: Early on 19 December 2019 a window cleaner found a chalked symbol on a pavement, apparently a Vodou veve for Papa Legba, with crossed keys, rum, cigarettes, a goat's skull and a black candle. A nearby business feared it was aimed at them. No explanation was found; coordinates are town-level (approx).

sources.name: Fortean Times (Feb 2020) – Occult crime, Pagan policemen and a Todmorden mystery

new.title: Standedge Tunnel, Marsden – sheep's heads and painted symbols
new.desc: On 31 May 1980 workmen found two sheep's heads and strange painted symbols about 1.5 miles inside the disused canal tunnels; a police search found nothing more. In the mid-1980s explorers saw white painted symbols, including a pentagram, in the chamber known as 'The Cathedral'. A 2010s Huddersfield Examiner look-back found no evidence of actual rituals.

sources.name: Huddersfield Examiner – Mystery of black magic rituals

new.title: St James's ('White Church'), Baildon – pentagram and arson attempt
new.desc: On Christmas Day (year not given in the online report) the church at the foot of Hollins Hill was found daubed with a 6ft pentagram and 'Hail Grimm', a rear window smashed and accelerant poured through the letterbox in an apparent attempt to burn it. The Christmas service went ahead without candles; no arrests were reported.

sources.name: Yorkshire Post – Shock at 'satanic' attack on historic church

new.title: Maggie Wall monument, Dunning
new.desc: A rough cairn-like monument about 6 m high, topped by a cross and painted 'Maggie Wall burnt here 1657 as a witch', stands about a mile west of Dunning. It is first recorded around 1800; no record of a Maggie Wall exists, and some historians think it a folly or cenotaph for the several Dunning women executed as witches. The inscription is repainted anonymously.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Maggie Wall
Undiscovered Scotland – Maggie Wall

new.title: Witches' Stone, Forres
new.desc: A stone by Victoria Road at the foot of Cluny Hill marks where, by tradition, a woman accused of witchcraft died after being rolled down the hill in a spiked barrel; its plaque says barrels came to rest and were then burned. Tradition also links it to witches who allegedly cursed King Duncan. The barrel story is legend rather than documented history.

sources.name: Forres Heritage Trust – Witches Stone
Aberdeenshire HER – MAB3401 Witches Stones, Forres

new.title: Maxwellton Cross, Paisley – grave of the 1697 Paisley witches
new.desc: After the Bargarran 'possession' accusations, seven people were hanged and burned at Gallow Green, Paisley, in June 1697 – among the last mass executions for witchcraft in western Europe. Their remains were buried at the Maxwellton Cross crossroads, and a horseshoe was later set in the road to guard against a curse they had reputedly laid on the town. A plaque now marks the spot in the junction.

sources.name: Paisley's Enchanted Threads – Maxwellton Cross
Wikipedia – Katherine Campbell (accused witch)

new.title: Pittenweem – the 1704–05 witch hunt and lynching
new.desc: In 1704 a teenage blacksmith's apprentice accused several Pittenweem women of bewitching him; they were held and tortured in the tolbooth. Janet Cornfoot escaped, was brought back from Leuchars and on 30 January 1705 was lynched by a mob at the harbour – stoned, swung from a ship's rope and crushed under a door weighted with stones. No one was ever tried; a 2012 proposal for a memorial was voted down. Pin at the harbour.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Pittenweem witches
Historic Environment Scotland blog – The Pittenweem witch hunt

new.title: Auldearn – Isobel Gowdie's 1662 confessions
new.desc: Between 13 April and 27 May 1662, probably in the Auldearn tolbooth, Isobel Gowdie of Lochloy gave four extraordinary confessions: a pact with the Devil at Auldearn kirk, a coven of thirteen, shapeshifting into hares, flights to feast with the Queen of Elphame, and clay images to harm the laird's sons. Forty-one people were arrested in consequence. Her fate is unrecorded. Pin on the parish church.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Isobel Gowdie
Survey of Scottish Witchcraft – case C/EGD/1558

new.title: Witches' Well, Castlehill, Edinburgh
new.desc: A small bronze fountain by John Duncan, commissioned by Patrick Geddes in 1894, commemorates people burned as witches in Edinburgh between 1479 and 1722, many on Castlehill – including Dr John Fian of the North Berwick trials. Its imagery of serpents and foxglove alludes to good and evil uses of knowledge.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Witches' Well, Edinburgh
Wikipedia – North Berwick witch trials

new.title: Witch's Stone, Littletown, Dornoch – Janet Horne
new.desc: Janet Horne, an elderly woman accused of riding her lame daughter as a pony to the Devil to be shod, was convicted by the sheriff and burned in tar at Dornoch in June 1727 (some sources say 1722) – the last legal execution for witchcraft in the British Isles. Her daughter escaped. A stone in Littletown marks the traditional site.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Janet Horne
Highland HER – MHG11675 Witch Stone, Little Town, Dornoch

new.title: Dunsapie Hill, Holyrood Park – pentagram and 'altar'
new.desc: A walker found a pentagram in a circle drawn in a white substance on secluded Dunsapie Hill, with eye-motif graffiti on nearby rocks; a local pagan shop owner suggested a winter-solstice rite using salt or ash. The year before, a concrete 'altar' and a metal plaque had been removed from Whinny Hill above St Margaret's Loch. Historic Environment Scotland treats damage in the scheduled park as heritage crime. Report undated online; coordinates approximate.

sources.name: Midlothian Advertiser / Edinburgh Evening News – Mystery surrounds disappearance of pagan symbol in Holyrood Park

new.title: Askeaton Hellfire Club
new.desc: The red-brick and stone clubhouse built around 1740 by the St Leger family stands, now ruined, within the bailey of Askeaton's Desmond castle on an island in the River Deel. A painting by James Worsdale shows the members – local gentry such as the Crokers of Ballingarde and Wyndham Quin of Adare – and the club had closed before 1800. Like other Irish Hellfire Clubs it was associated with drinking and gaming; devil-worship stories are lore. Pin on the castle.

sources.name: Limerick.ie – The Hell Fire Club, Askeaton
Kilkenny Castle – Drunkenness, debauchery and devil worship: Ireland's Hellfire Clubs

new.title: Loftus Hall – the Devil at the card table
new.desc: Legend says that around 1766, while the Tottenham family lived here, a storm-bound stranger joined a card game; when Anne Tottenham stooped for a dropped card she saw a cloven hoof, and he vanished through the roof in a ball of fire. Anne, who died in 1775, is said to haunt the house. The tale parallels the Dublin Hellfire Club legend and is folklore; the house closed to visitors in 2020 and is privately owned.

sources.name: The Irish Road Trip – Loftus Hall

new.title: Knowehead House, Islandmagee – the 1711 witch trial
new.desc: After Mary Dunbar suffered fits at Knowehead House in 1711, eight women – Janet Carson, Janet Latimer, Janet Main, Janet Millar, Margaret Mitchell, Catherine McCalmond, Janet Liston and Elizabeth Sellor – were tried at Carrickfergus in March 1711, Ireland's last witch trial. Records are lost, but they were probably sentenced to a year's imprisonment and the pillory. Pin on the house site.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Islandmagee witch trial
Islandmagee Witches 1711 project – history

new.title: Youghal – the 'Witch of Youghal', 1661
new.desc: Florence Newton was accused of bewitching a servant girl with a kiss at Christmas 1660 (fits, vomiting pins and nails) and of killing her gaoler by sorcery. She was imprisoned in March 1661 and tried at the Cork Assizes in September 1661; recent research suggests she died before the trial concluded. Coordinates are town-level (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Florence Newton
Irish Legal News – The Witch of Youghal

new.title: Holy Cross Church, Kenmare – pentagram graffiti
new.desc: Mass-goers arriving for 9am Mass on Sunday 13 February 2022 found the front of the limestone church sprayed in red with a pentagram-like symbol and black writing in an unknown language. Gardaí treated it as criminal damage; no arrests were reported.

sources.name: Irish Catholic – Gardaí investigating after satanic vandalism of Kenmare church
BreakingNews.ie – Gardaí investigating after mass-goers find church front defaced in Kerry

new.title: Smelt Monument, Castletown – Margaret Inequane burned 1617
new.place: Market Square, Castletown, Isle of Man
new.desc: In 1617 Margaret Inequane and her son John Cubon were burned at the stake for witchcraft beside the market cross in Castletown; lore says she was caught performing a crop-fertility charm. It is the only recorded Manx witchcraft execution – later cases went to church courts. A plaque on the Smelt Monument, which stands on the site, commemorates them.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Margaret Inequane
As Manx as the Hills – The witch hunt: witch burning on the Isle of Man

new.title: St Mary's Church, Bottesford – the 'sorcerye' tomb
new.desc: The monument to Francis Manners, 6th Earl of Rutland, records that his two sons 'died in their infancy by wicked practise and sorcerye' – believed to be the only English tomb naming witchcraft as a cause of death. The Belvoir Castle servants Joan Flower and her daughters were blamed: Joan died on the way to trial, and Margaret and Philippa Flower were hanged at Lincoln on 11 March 1619.

sources.name: Historic England – Heritage Calling: 5 chilling tales from churches
Wikipedia – Witches of Belvoir
Bottesford Living History – The Bottesford Witches

new.title: Lincoln Castle – Belvoir witches hanged 1619
new.desc: Margaret and Philippa Flower, former servants at Belvoir Castle accused of killing the Earl of Rutland's heirs by sorcery, were tried before judges Hobart and Bromley and hanged at Lincoln on 11 March 1619. Their mother Joan had died at Ancaster on the way to trial, reportedly choking on bread she had asked for as a test of innocence.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Witches of Belvoir

new.title: St Mary's Church, Akenham – the 'Devil's grave'
new.desc: A broken tombstone in this redundant medieval churchyard is known as the Devil's grave: legend says walking anticlockwise round the church thirteen times will summon him. The church was also the scene of the 1878 'Akenham burial case' over an unbaptised child, which went to the High Court and fed into the Burial Laws Amendment Act 1880.

sources.name: Historic England – Heritage Calling: 5 chilling tales from churches
Wikipedia – Akenham

new.title: Christchurch Garden Theatre & Ashrama Hall – Gardner's 'New Forest coven'
new.desc: The Rosicrucian Order Crotona Fellowship built its wooden Ashrama Hall (1936) and the 'First Rosicrucian Theatre in England' (1938) near Christchurch. Gerald Gardner joined the group, and scholars suggest some members were the circle he later called the 'New Forest coven', into which he claimed initiation in 1939 – a founding story of Wicca. Coordinates are for Somerford (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Rosicrucian Order Crotona Fellowship
Wikipedia – New Forest coven
Christchurch History Society – Christchurch Garden Theatre

new.title: Chalice Orchard, Glastonbury – Dion Fortune's sanctuary
new.desc: In 1924 the occultist Dion Fortune's group acquired an old orchard at the foot of Glastonbury Tor, adding a hut, veranda and chalets; it served as a summer guest house and lecture centre, and from 1931 as the Society of the Inner Light's 'Sanctuary'. Fortune died in January 1946 and is buried in Glastonbury. Coordinates approximate (Wellhouse Lane area).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Dion Fortune
Wikipedia – Society of the Inner Light

new.title: Bricket Wood – Gardner's 'Witches' Cottage'
new.desc: In 1945 Gerald Gardner bought a plot at the Fiveacres naturist club and re-erected a 16th-century cottage there, decorated inside with magical sigils. From about 1946 it was the ritual space of the Bricket Wood coven, with Gardner as High Priest and 'Dafo' as High Priestess – the first Gardnerian Wicca coven. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Bricket Wood coven

new.title: 67–69 Chancery Lane – Crowley's ritual flat
new.desc: Around 1899 Aleister Crowley took a flat at 67–69 Chancery Lane, where he and Allan Bennett performed Goetic evocations. Pin at no. 67 (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Aleister Crowley

new.title: 36 Blythe Road – Golden Dawn 'Vault of the Adepts'
new.desc: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn kept its ritual Vault of the Adepts at 36 Blythe Road. In 1900 Crowley, acting for MacGregor Mathers, tried to seize it from the London lodge (the 'Battle of Blythe Road'); a court ruled for the lodge. Coordinates are for Blythe Road (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Aleister Crowley

new.title: Caxton Hall – Crowley's Rites of Eleusis
new.desc: In October–November 1910 Crowley staged the Rites of Eleusis, a series of public magical performances, at Caxton Hall; the press attacked them as blasphemous.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Aleister Crowley

new.title: 124 Victoria Street – A∴A∴ headquarters
new.desc: From 1907 the magical order A∴A∴, founded by Crowley and George Cecil Jones, used 124 Victoria Street as its headquarters and temple. Coordinates are for Victoria Street (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Aleister Crowley

new.title: Ashdown Park Hotel, Coulsdon – Crowley's Abramelin rituals
new.desc: Around 1907 Crowley and George Cecil Jones carried out Abramelin rituals at the Ashdown Park Hotel in Coulsdon. Coordinates are for Ashdown Park (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Aleister Crowley

new.title: Warboys – the Witches of Warboys
new.desc: From November 1589 the Throckmorton children and servants at Warboys suffered fits and accused their elderly neighbour Alice Samuel; when Lady Cromwell died after visiting her, the charge became murder. In April 1593 Alice Samuel, her husband John and daughter Agnes were convicted at Huntingdon and hanged. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Witches of Warboys

new.title: Heavitree gallows, Exeter – the Bideford witches hanged 1682
new.place: St Luke's Campus, Heavitree Road, Exeter
new.desc: Temperance Lloyd, Mary Trembles and Susannah Edwards of Bideford were convicted at the Exeter Assizes largely on hearsay and hanged at the Heavitree gallows on 25 August 1682 – often called the last executions for witchcraft in England. The gallows site is now a car park at the University of Exeter's St Luke's Campus; a plaque at Exeter Castle names them.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Bideford witch trial

new.title: Mistley Heath – burial of the Witchfinder General
new.desc: Matthew Hopkins began his witch-hunt in nearby Manningtree in March 1644; with John Stearne he drove the trials of 1645–47, including Chelmsford, where nineteen women were hanged. He died at Manningtree on 12 August 1647 and was buried the same day at St Mary's, Mistley Heath (the church has gone). Tradition says he owned the Thorn Inn at Mistley. Coordinates are village-level (approx).

sources.name: Wikipedia – Matthew Hopkins

new.title: Admirals Park, Chelmsford – witch-trial memorial
new.desc: A plaque and oak tree dedicated on 1 December 2022 near South Primrose Hill, a historic execution site, remember the more than 100 people accused of witchcraft in Chelmsford in the 16th–17th centuries – from Agnes Waterhouse, hanged on 29 July 1566, to the Hopkins-era trials of 1645.

sources.name: Chelmsford City Life – Admirals Park memorial for witch trial victims

new.title: St Mary's Catholic Church, Great Yarmouth – satanic emblem on altar
new.desc: During Holy Week 2018 (the night of Tuesday 27 March) CCTV showed a young man lighting small fires inside the church, trying to burn an icon and leaving a satanist emblem on the altar; months earlier a satanic picture had been left at the foot of a cross. Norfolk Police arrested a 17-year-old, and the bishop re-dedicated the altar about two months later.

sources.name: Crux – Satanic vandalism blights Holy Week at Catholic parish in England
Crux – Bishop re-dedicates altar two months after satanic attack

new.title: St John's, Stratford – pentagrams, '666' and arson
new.desc: In late June 2019 four doors of St John's, Stratford, were scored with pentagrams and '666' and burning paper pushed against the main door; nearby St Matthew's, West Ham, suffered three arson attempts in 24 hours and had '666' scratched on its door, and a Forest Gate church was also marked. The Met arrested a 27-year-old man on suspicion of arson and criminal damage.

sources.name: Church Times – Man arrested after churches vandalised (5 July 2019)

new.title: Kewlake Lane, Cadnam – ewe impaled with hay cross
new.desc: On 2 January 2020 a ewe was found stabbed to death (eight knife wounds) beside a pitchfork, with an upside-down cross made of hay on its fleece – part of the New Forest series that began with pentagram-marked sheep and the Bramshaw church graffiti in November 2019. Three more sheep were found dead on 16–20 January. A Winchester man arrested later that month was released without charge.

sources.name: The Scottish Farmer – Black magic blamed for 'satanic' slaughter of sheep
Yahoo News – 'Occult' killings: man arrested over 'Satanic' sheep deaths in New Forest (Jan 2020)

new.title: St Michael and All Angels, Lyndhurst – deer heads left at church
new.desc: A sika deer's head was found outside the church in 2021, and on Wednesday 15 January 2025 a walker found another severed deer head in the churchyard – the latest of a string of New Forest animal remains left at churches and landmarks (Bramshaw 2019–22, Burley 2024). No arrests were reported.

sources.name: Bournemouth Buzz – Latest animal mutilation in string of disturbing incidents (Jan 2025)

notes:
Research pass 2026-10-29 (web only). 'improve' entries key on the exact existing titles; lat/lon given only where verified: British Listed Buildings/Historic England/Cadw records (Clophill – unchanged, Bawsey, Babingley, Bix, Gyffin, Conwy St Mary), Coflein NGR (Ffynnon Elian, ~1.6 km from old estimate), Northern Antiquarian OS grid ref (Thor's Stone), OpenStreetMap (King's Men circle, Bramshaw St Peter, Stagbury Hill summit, Montpelier Hill summit, Meon Hill summit). NOT re-pinned: Malkin Tower Farm (true site unknown; three candidates) and Malin church (sources never name the building). Stagbury caveat: press said only 'trig pillar near St Peter's Church, Bramshaw'; the hill name comes from the existing entry – pin moved to the OSM Stagbury Hill summit ~2 km E of the church. Meon Hill pin is the summit; the 1945 killing was in 'Hillground' field on the slopes (exact field unlocated).
Corrections: Culdaff church = St Mary's, Bocan, attacked Sun 24 Jul 2016 (TheJournal.ie), so the Inishowen series began late July, not August. The Dyserth '1637' case was NOT a witch trial – it was a sorcery slur in a 1638 Court of Arches pew dispute. RCAHMW's 'Welsh Witches' page links Gwen ferch Ellis's witnesses to 'St Cewydd's Church, Dyserth' (NPRN 300471) – St Cewydd's is actually at Disserth, Radnorshire, so I did not use that claim; the Dyserth entry is pinned to St Bridget's (Flintshire). Gloddaith is spelt Gloddaeth in Cadw/BLB.
Naming policy applied: convicted/executed historic defendants are named (Inequane, Boughton 1656, Baguley, Samuels, Bideford three, Flower sisters, Islandmagee eight, Llannor siblings, Marged ferch Rhisiart). Acquitted or never-tried archive defendants are NOT named (Penley 1657, Llanasa 1656/1690, Dyserth 1637, Samlesbury 1612, Pembrokeshire/Montgomery cases). Exceptions are long-dead public historical figures known chiefly through their own memorials or Wikipedia articles (Isobel Gowdie, Janet Cornfoot, Florence Newton, Janet Horne, Maggie Wall) – drop these names if you want strict compliance. Modern victims and suspects are never named (Meon Hill victim, Llanrwst grave, New Forest arrestee, Highgate 1974 convict).
Not added (insufficient/unsuitable sourcing): Guiting Power, Bramber, Leigh-on-Sea 1963 (no source found; Leigh only has a TV ghost-show 'witches' story), a 'Kilkenny Hellfire Club' (none found – Kilkenny's occult site is Kyteler's, already in), Alderley Edge (only wizard legend / folklore pages, no ritual incident), Bidston Hill/Flaybrick/Liverpool/Manchester (no sourced occult incidents found), Colwyn Bay 1989 'coven recruiting with sex and drugs' allegation (unverified allegation against unnamed people), Celbridge 2013 and Leyland 2025 church graffiti (no occult content), Witney woods hedgehog/robes report (undated, anonymous), Cleethorpes lamb (councillor speculation only), Dartmoor 'satanic pony' 2012 (police found natural causes). Already in other layers: Ffynnon Eilian (Llaneilian, Anglesey) and Ffynnon Gapan (cursing wells) are in wells_wales.json; Pendle Hill & Lancaster Castle also in paranormal.json.
Undated items: Caerwys (Daily Post undated), Wigan St Mark's (Thursday 27 June – fits 2019 but year not printed), Baildon (Christmas Day, year not printed), Holyrood Park (undated online) – dates left blank rather than guessed. Wikipedia API was rate-limited from this host; facts were checked via WebFetch of the pages instead.
